questions.stem: In which Parva of the Mahābhārata does the narrative of the Vyādha Gītā take place?
stem_variants: Where is the Vyādha Gītā situated within the Mahābhārata?
questions.explanation: The Vyādha Gītā occurs in the Vana Parva (Forest Book) of the Mahābhārata, narrated during the Pāṇḍavas' period of exile.
questions.source_quote: Story is in Vana Parva... in the time when the Pāṇḍavas were in exile.

questions.stem: How did the housewife shatter the pride of the young Brāhmaṇa who demanded immediate alms?
stem_variants: What caused the young ascetic to be stunned when the housewife asked him to wait?
options: She revealed she knew he had burned a crane to ashes with his angry glare in the forest.
She cursed him to lose all the mystical powers accumulated through his tapas.
She recited the Vedas more fluently than he could and challenged him to debate.
She summoned Dharmavyādha magically to reprimand him on the spot.
distractor_pool: She cursed him to lose all the mystical powers accumulated through his tapas.
She recited the Vedas more fluently than he could and challenged him to debate.
She summoned Dharmavyādha magically to reprimand him on the spot.
questions.answer: She revealed she knew he had burned a crane to ashes with his angry glare in the forest.
accepted_answers: She revealed she knew he had burned a crane to ashes with his angry glare in the forest.
questions.explanation: When the Brāhmaṇa flared up in anger because she made him wait while feeding her tired husband, she smiled and asked: 'Do you think I am a crane that you can burn me up?'
questions.source_quote: She smiled and said, 'Do you think I am a crane that you can burn me up?'

questions.stem: What core philosophical principle did Dharmavyādha use to justify his profession as a butcher?
stem_variants: According to Dharmavyādha, why is his gruesome work not a spiritual disqualifier?
options: No duty is inherently impure or ugly when performed with detachment and devotion as service.
Slaughtering animals is a Vedic sacrifice exempt from all karmic repercussion.
Birth in a specific caste cancels the spiritual law of karma altogether.
Ascetic forest life is spiritually forbidden for anyone born into a trade.
distractor_pool: Slaughtering animals is a Vedic sacrifice exempt from all karmic repercussion.
Birth in a specific caste cancels the spiritual law of karma altogether.
Ascetic forest life is spiritually forbidden for anyone born into a trade.
questions.answer: No duty is inherently impure or ugly when performed with detachment and devotion as service.
accepted_answers: No duty is inherently impure or ugly when performed with detachment and devotion as service.
questions.explanation: Dharmavyādha stated: 'No duty is ugly, no duty is impure. Birth placed me in these circumstances... I am unattached and try to do my duty well.' Treating work as worship transforms any duty into Karma Yoga.
questions.source_quote: No duty is ugly, no duty is impure. Birth placed me in these circumstances. I learned this trade as a boy; I am unattached and try to do my duty well.

questions.stem: In the comparison cited from Amma, how are King Dakṣa's yajña and Arjuna's Kurukṣetra contrasted regarding inner attitude?
stem_variants: What contrast does Amma draw between Dakṣa's sacrifice and Arjuna's battlefield?
options: Dakṣa turned a holy sacrifice into a battleground through ego, while Arjuna turned a battleground into worship through faith.
Dakṣa renounced action prematurely, while Arjuna abandoned devotion to embrace mere warfare.
Dakṣa attained enlightenment through rigid rites, while Arjuna attained it by fleeing battle to the forest.
Dakṣa prioritized family duty above all, while Arjuna abandoned his kinsmen for ascetic powers.
distractor_pool: Dakṣa renounced action prematurely, while Arjuna abandoned devotion to embrace mere warfare.
Dakṣa attained enlightenment through rigid rites, while Arjuna attained it by fleeing battle to the forest.
Dakṣa prioritized family duty above all, while Arjuna abandoned his kinsmen for ascetic powers.
questions.answer: Dakṣa turned a holy sacrifice into a battleground through ego, while Arjuna turned a battleground into worship through faith.
accepted_answers: Dakṣa turned a holy sacrifice into a battleground through ego, while Arjuna turned a battleground into worship through faith.
questions.explanation: Amma contrasts Dakṣa's yajña, which deteriorated into a violent battlefield due to pride and audacity, with Arjuna, whose surrender and faith in Kṛṣṇa turned the battlefield of Kurukṣetra into a sacred place of worship.
questions.source_quote: contrasted Dakṣa's yajña, which became a battlefield through his audacity, with Arjuna who, through faith in Kṛṣṇa, turned Kurukṣetra into a place of worship.

questions.stem: How does Swami Vivekananda's evaluation of the Vyādha Gītā reframe the classical concept of Advaitic renunciation (sannyāsa)?
stem_variants: According to Swami Vivekananda, what does the Vyādha Gītā demonstrate regarding the true nature of renunciation?
options: Because the all-pervading Self is already within, authentic renunciation does not necessitate fleeing domestic life for the forest.
Advaita necessitates complete physical withdrawal from social karma before true knowledge can be assimilated.
Householders can only attain secondary merits, whereas liberation is exclusively reserved for monastic sannyāsins.
Ritual penances and acquisition of yogic siddhis must always precede the practice of non-dual meditation.
distractor_pool: Advaita necessitates complete physical withdrawal from social karma before true knowledge can be assimilated.
Householders can only attain secondary merits, whereas liberation is exclusively reserved for monastic sannyāsins.
Ritual penances and acquisition of yogic siddhis must always precede the practice of non-dual meditation.
questions.answer: Because the all-pervading Self is already within, authentic renunciation does not necessitate fleeing domestic life for the forest.
accepted_answers: Because the all-pervading Self is already within, authentic renunciation does not necessitate fleeing domestic life for the forest.
questions.explanation: Swami Vivekananda explains that the Vyādha Gītā reaches the heights of Advaita: since the all-pervading Divine Self resides within, renunciation does not mean abandoning parents or home to dwell in a forest; one can remain a householder and realize the highest spiritual truth through selfless duty.
questions.source_quote: Swami Vivekananda says the Vyādha Gītā contains the heights of Advaita, which preaches renunciation; but when the all-pervading Self is within, renunciation is not leaving home for the forest.
